title: A reading list for karyakartas
author: Editorial Desk
summary: Ten places to start for anyone who wants to understand BMS and Indian labour law, with notes on what each offers and how to read it.
body:
A union karyakarta is expected to know a great deal: the law, the history of the movement, the ideas behind the organisation, and the facts of the industry. Nobody can learn all of that at once, and nobody should rely on forwarded messages for it. This post offers ten places to start, with a note on what each one is good for and how to read it. We have looked at each of these ourselves, but sites and documents change, so please check each one yourself and note the date on which you read it.

## Ideas and history of BMS

**1. The Dattopant Thengadi Archive (dbthengadi.in).** This site gathers the life, writings and tributes of the founder of BMS. Its sections include Books, Articles, Tribute, Videos, Gallery and Audios. The catalogue includes titles in English such as *Third Way*, *The Perspective*, *Labour Policy* and *Focus: On the Socio-Economic Problems*, together with Hindi and Marathi books, and tribute pieces by writers such as S. Gurumurthy and C. K. Saji Narayanan ([Dattopant Thengadi Archive](https://dbthengadi.in)). It is the right place to begin if you have never read him directly.

**2. *The Onward March of BMS*.** A history of the organisation's early decades, available as a PDF on the Thengadi archive. The text describes the climate before 1955, when recognised central labour organisations were wings of political parties, and then the founding convention at Bhopal on 23 July 1955. It also traces the early years, including the difficulties of victimisation and scepticism that the first activists faced, and BMS's role in events through the 1960s and 1970s ([The Onward March of BMS](https://cdn.dbthengadi.in/scan/The_Onward_March_OF_BMS.pdf)). The excerpt we read does not name its author or the year of publication, so mention that if you quote it.

**3. *Consumer: A Sovereign without Sovereignty* by D. B. Thengadi.** First published in November 1986 by the Akhil Bharatiya Grahak Panchayat, Nagpur, as study material for its first All India Study Class. Its main argument is that consumers are called sovereign but in practice have little real power, and that peasants, workers and consumers are exploited by middlemen and profiteers and should not be set against each other. It also discusses consumer co-operatives, consumer law and practical reforms ([Consumer: A Sovereign without Sovereignty](https://vvgnli.gov.in/sites/default/files/Consumer%20A%20Sovereign%20without%20Sovereignty.pdf)). It is a good model of how to build an argument from facts and examples.

**4. The BMS website (bms.org.in).** Here you will find news, statements and resolutions. Two useful examples are the press release on the Central Executive meeting of August 2025, which sets out BMS's position on the Codes and asks for the Indian Labour Conference to be convened ([BMS press release](https://www.bms.org.in/?p=8936)), and the statement of 31 January 2026 on why BMS would not join a general strike ([BMS statement](https://www.bms.org.in/?p=9332)). The website also gives the organisation's basic information: it was founded on 23 July 1955, and its motto is "Nationalise the Labour, Labourise the Industry, Industrialise the Nation" ([BMS website](https://www.bms.org.in/?p=388)).

## Law and policy

**5. The Ministry of Labour and Employment (labour.gov.in).** This is the source for Acts, Codes, notifications, press releases and FAQs. The Ministry's release of 21 November 2025 summarises the four Codes, and the FAQs it has issued explain points such as the floor wage, gratuity and the contract labour threshold ([Labour Ministry release](https://labour.gov.in/sites/default/files/pib2192463.pdf); [SCC Online on the FAQs](https://www.scconline.com/blog/post/2026/01/03/labour-ministry-issued-faqs-on-the-labour-codes/)). Read the original text first, then the FAQ.

**6. India Code (indiacode.nic.in).** The Government's digital repository of central and State Acts. Use it when you need the exact wording of a section, because summaries and news reports can leave out qualifications. Always check whether you are reading the current version.

**7. PRS Legislative Research (prsindia.org).** PRS publishes plain summaries of Bills and Codes. Its summary of the Code on Wages, for instance, explains the floor wage, how minimum wages must be reviewed at least every five years, the 50 per cent cap on deductions, and the bonus provisions ([PRS: Code on Wages, 2019](https://prsindia.org/billtrack/prs-products/prs-bill-summary-3305)). It is a good way to understand the structure of a law before reading the full text.

**8. The International Labour Organization (ilo.org).** The ILO's standards, reports and data put Indian questions in a world setting. For example, India ratifies conventions voluntarily and has said it prefers to implement first and ratify later, so the ILO's NORMLEX database is the place to check which conventions India has actually ratified ([Arthapedia: International Labour Standards and India](https://ies.gov.in/arthapedia/concept/international-labour-standards-and-india)). The ILO's Convention No. 144 on tripartite consultation is also the background to BMS's repeated calls to convene the Indian Labour Conference, which last met in 2015 ([Drishti IAS](https://www.drishtiias.com/daily-updates/daily-news-analysis/indian-labour-conference)).

**9. V.V. Giri National Labour Institute (vvgnli.gov.in).** The Government's labour research and training institute keeps a library of reports and historical documents. Among those we read are the pamphlet *Bharatiya Mazdoor Sangh At a Glance*, which has dates and verification figures ([VVGNLI: BMS at a Glance](https://vvgnli.gov.in/sites/default/files/Bharatiya%20Mazdoor%20Sangh%20At%20a%20Glance.pdf)), and *Six Decades of Textile Labour Association, Ahmedabad*, an account of the Gandhian union in Ahmedabad ([VVGNLI: Six Decades of TLA](https://vvgnli.gov.in/sites/default/files/Six%20Decades%20of%20Textile%20Labour%20Association%2C%20Ahmedabad%20%281917-1977%29.pdf)). The Indian Labour Archives also hosts many such documents.

**10. The Constitution of India.** The text that frames all labour law. For a karyakarta, a few provisions are worth reading in the original. Article 19(1)(c) protects the right to form associations or unions. Article 23 prohibits trafficking and forced labour, including *begar*. In Part IV, the Directive Principles, Articles 39, 41, 42 and 43 deal with the State's duty on livelihood, work, humane conditions of work, maternity relief and a living wage, and Article 43A, inserted by the Forty-second Amendment in 1976, speaks of workers' participation in the management of industries ([Article 19](https://constitutionofindia.net/articles/article-19-protection-of-certain-rights-regarding-freedom-of-speech-etc/); [Article 23](https://constitutionofindia.net/articles/article-23-prohibition-of-traffic-in-human-beings-and-forced-labour/); [Article 43A](https://constitutionofindia.net/articles/article-43a-participation-of-workers-in-management-of-industries/); [Part IV](https://constitutionofindia.net/parts/part-iv/)). Article 24, on child labour, is also in this group of fundamental rights.

## How to read

1. **Start with the original text.** Read the section, the notification or the book itself. Commentary comes afterwards.
2. **Read actively.** Keep a notebook. For each reading, write three lines: what it says, what you disagree with or do not understand, and where it applies to your union.
3. **Note the date and version.** Labour law is changing quickly, with the Codes in force since 21 November 2025, Central rules notified in May 2026, and State rules still arriving. A summary from last year may already be out of date.
4. **Check the author's standpoint.** A Government release, a trade union pamphlet, a law-firm newsletter and an academic paper each have a purpose. Using several kinds of source, and noticing what each leaves out, makes you a better advocate for your members.
5. **Discuss.** A reading circle of five or six karyakartas, meeting once a fortnight, will learn more than the same people reading alone.

## A four-week plan

- **Week 1:** the BMS pamphlet and the first chapters of *The Onward March of BMS*.
- **Week 2:** the Labour Ministry's summary of the four Codes and the FAQs.
- **Week 3:** the Thengadi booklet on consumers, or another of his short works.
- **Week 4:** the Constitutional provisions listed above, and a discussion of how one of them applies in your industry.

## Share your suggestions

If a book or paper has helped you, tell us. We will consider adding it to the Downloads page of this website, after checking its source and availability.
